doc.title: Bob Haggart interviewed by Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, September 22, 1995

title: Swinging at slow tempos
summary: Basie's laid-back time and how to play slow with lead-in notes and double-time feeling.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Sometimes too much precision can stop it from swinging, if it’s rigid.

You listen to the Basie band. They used to lean so far back you thought they were going to — they’re not slowing down but it seems like it. Some of those real slow things you know? It’s very hard to play slow and keep it swinging.
Because the tone is so exposed.

I want to ask you something about playing the bass and playing slowly. Because a string bass, unlike amplified bass guitar, you only have your physical enunciation of the string. And obviously no matter how hard you hit it there’s a certain amount of decay in between notes. But it’s the sustain of the notes that drives it. So that has to be a lot of your particular technique to keep a band so instead of playing notes — thud-thud-thud, you play a phrase — ka-toom-toom-toom.

That’s right, you have to. You have to preface the notes with little lead-ins, especially when it’s real slow — te-te-te-bamm — or a little da-dit-en-dit-en-duh. You can do triplets, you could do sixteenths, you could do something. As long as the downbeats are where they’re supposed to be.
You have to nail it down.

That’s right. You’re swinging them all slowly, you’ve got to swing, because you’re beating double time anyway, if you’re playing very slow you’re sort of beating in twelve you know, you think in twelve. Four sets of sixteenths. So it’s really double time, but you don’t play double time, you think double time. Or else you think in triplets. So it’s back and forth, you know. I don’t know whether that makes sense or not.
